name: Yule
walkingTradition: Torch processions through forest paths in the long northern dark, gathering around fire and evergreen.

name: Saturnalia
walkingTradition: Public revel and exchange of small candles called sigillaria as the sun bottomed and turned. Streets given over to walking and feasting.

name: Dongzhi 冬至
walkingTradition: Family gathering and temple visits. Eating tangyuan — round dumplings — to mark the year's deepest dark and the return of yang.
sourceNote: Stepanchuk and Wong, Mooncakes and Hungry Ghosts (1991).

name: Inti Raymi
walkingTradition: Multi-day procession from Sacsayhuaman to the sacred fields above Cusco. Walking the route at dawn to 'tie the sun' against further descent.
sourceNote: Bauer and Dearborn, Astronomy and Empire in the Ancient Andes (1995).

name: Nowruz نوروز
walkingTradition: Sizdah Bedar — on the thirteenth day of Nowruz, families walk together into nature to scatter sprouted lentils into running water. The walk back home is the renewal.

name: Ostara
sourceNote: Walking-tradition unattested in primary sources; Bede's brief 8th c. mention names a goddess but describes no rite. Modern Ostara observances are reconstructed.

name: Litha
walkingTradition: Bonfire vigils on hilltops the night before; walking from low ground to high ground to greet the longest sun.
sourceNote: Hutton, Stations of the Sun (1996). Modern observances draw on these older British practices.

name: Midsommar
walkingTradition: Walking to a maypole in the country, dancing around it through the night that never quite gets dark. Picking seven kinds of flower in silence on the walk home.

name: Chuseok 추석
calendarSystem: 15th day of the 8th lunar month (≈ near autumn equinox)
walkingTradition: Beolcho — walking out to ancestral graves to clear them. Charye — returning home to share the harvest and watch the round moon rise.
sourceNote: Lee, Korean Folk Belief and Folktales (2008).

name: Mid-Autumn Festival 中秋節
walkingTradition: Lantern walks at dusk under the harvest moon. Children carry paper lanterns through neighborhoods and parks. Adults walk to high places to see the moon rise complete.
sourceNote: Stepanchuk and Wong, Mooncakes and Hungry Ghosts (1991).

name: Mabon
sourceNote: Modern observance named in 1970 by Aidan Kelly; no documented historical antecedent under this name.
